chunks: When you run out of GPIOs. The question: What can I do if I don't have enough GPIOs?
When a microcontroller runs out of GPIO pins, you can often get more without changing it. The first question is whether you can free up pins, or pick a chip with a bigger package.
If not, you add a small chip that turns a few pins into many. Each trick trades pins for time, extra parts, or more complex software.
Imagine one loading door feeding eight shelves through a conveyor belt. You slide items onto the belt one at a time.
When all eight are in place, you press a single button, and every shelf locks at once. But it takes eight steps instead of one. That is the trade: fewer pins, more time.
A decision path for choosing a technique. Notice the first question is not "which chip?" but whether the constraint can be removed.
Shift register: a chip with a row of storage cells that you fill one bit at a time. It turns a few pins into 8 or more outputs, such as the 74HC595.
Latch: a pulse that copies all the bits to the outputs at once, so they do not flicker while you load.
I/O expander: a chip that adds 8 or 16 extra GPIO pins, controlled over a two-wire (I2C) or four-wire (SPI) bus.
Key matrix: wiring buttons in rows and columns, so a few pins read many buttons.
A 74HC595 needs three microcontroller pins: data, clock and latch. It gives 8 outputs. Chain four of them on the same three pins, and you have 32 outputs.
Sending 32 bits at a 1 megahertz clock takes 32 microseconds. For buttons, a 4 by 4 matrix reads 16 keys with only 8 pins.
An I2C expander can add 16 pins on two wires, but each update takes roughly 100 microseconds, so it is too slow for fast signals. That is the whole idea.
"First I'd see if I can free pins or step up to a bigger package.

Otherwise: for outputs a 74HC595 shift register turns three pins into eight outputs and chains for more; for inputs a 74HC165; for both, an I2C or SPI I/O expander like the MCP23017 gives 16 pins on two wires.
For buttons and LEDs I'd use a matrix, so 8 pins read 16 keys, Charlieplexing for LEDs, or a resistor ladder on one ADC pin. A decoder gives chip selects.
The cost is speed, CPU time and firmware complexity."
